items.title: [phys.org] UN warns warming will breach 1.5C as COP31 opens Monday
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The United Nations says global warming will exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold as nearly 200 countries prepare to begin the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9. Climate scientists say the rate of warming has effectively doubled over the past decade. October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to become the second year to exceed 1.5C, after 2024. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said the world must now limit how far temperatures rise beyond that level and blamed political leaders for failing to act. The Nov. 9-20 talks are expected to focus on fulfilling earlier promises to move away from fossil fuels and on funding for poorer countries facing climate impacts. Turkey is promoting a goal to increase electricity’s share of global energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035. Developed countries have resisted further funding commitments, and the Trump administration is not taking part in negotiations.

items.title: [npr.org] Alaska Native villages remain displaced a year after Typhoon Halong
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A year after the remnants of Typhoon Halong destroyed homes and infrastructure in western Alaska, residents of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok remain displaced as repairs continue, with many unsure when they can return. The October 2025 storm affected more than 40 communities, and about 1,500 people were evacuated from Kwigillingok, Kipnuk and Nightmute. Alaska officials estimate that federal aid will make most Kipnuk homes livable by Thanksgiving, but say some residents need replacement housing. The state is seeking more funding. Both Kipnuk and Kwigillingok voted to relocate to higher ground, but current disaster funding is not designed to pay for moving the communities.

items.title: [climatechangenews.com] COP17 urges subsidy cuts as nature finance gap persists before COP31
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Governments at the U.N. biodiversity summit, COP17, agreed to accelerate efforts to cut subsidies that damage nature, including support for fossil fuels, but left unresolved how to fund conservation. Nearly 200 countries adopted the Yerevan Pathway in Armenia after the first review found the world off track on almost all biodiversity goals for 2030. The agreement calls for countries to revise their biodiversity plans to address gaps in marine, coastal and inland-water protection and accelerate efforts to reduce harmful incentives by at least $500 billion a year by 2030. Developed countries missed a commitment to provide at least $20 billion annually for nature by 2025, while environmental funding is projected to fall 27% over 2026-30, Carbon Brief reported. Organizers said governments, philanthropies and investors announced more than $1.8 billion in nature finance at the summit, compared with the framework’s goal of mobilizing $200 billion a year by 2030. Countries invited non-donor states to express interest in joining the donor list, but deferred a decision on the structure of a permanent post-2030 financing mechanism until COP18 in Quito in 2028. The U.N. climate conference COP31 begins in Antalya, Türkiye, on Nov. 9.

items.title: [tygodnik-rolniczy.pl] German farmer plans 340-hectare shift from grain to silphium
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Holger Peters, a farmer in Schleswig-Holstein, plans to replace grain production on his 340 hectares of arable land with perennial silphium over the next two years. He has planted 125 hectares so far. He says grain production has become barely profitable, while silphium can supply his biogas plant and may also provide a peat substitute for horticultural growing media. Polish cabbage and potato growers are also reporting weak returns: cabbage for processing is selling at about 50 groszy per kilogram, while wholesale potato prices in Łódź ranged from 53 groszy to 1.07 zlotys per kilogram on Oct. 30. Potato farmers have sought higher fuel-tax refunds, but the agriculture ministry has instead pointed to promotional campaigns with retailers.

items.title: [tagesspiegel.de] Bird flu risk rises as 6,000 turkeys culled in northern Germany
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Germany’s Friedrich Loeffler Institute raised its bird-flu risk ratings for spread among wild birds and entry into poultry farms from “moderate” to “high” as an outbreak led to the culling of about 6,000 turkeys at a farm in Rostock district, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The state said the outbreak at the Wattmannshagen farm was its first poultry-farm case of the season. In Brandenburg, officials confirmed the autumn’s first case in a wild goose in Oder-Spree district. The institute reported that cases in wild birds and poultry had risen since October after a quieter period through September, with bird migration and falling temperatures contributing to the spread. A separate outbreak affected 6,000 turkeys in Lower Saxony’s Aurich district, while farms in Schleswig-Holstein also reported infections. The institute said it could not predict how severe this season would be.

items.title: [abcnews.com] Swift telescope shutdown ends rapid alerts for cosmic explosions
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

NASA shut down its Swift Observatory in late October after it could no longer hold steady enough for observations, ending a 22-year mission to detect gamma-ray bursts, supernovas and other high-energy events. Over its mission, Swift recorded more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars.

The Trump administration will not take part in the negotiations, although a U.S. congressional delegation is expected to attend.

items.title: [cisa.gov] U.S. agencies warn hackers are targeting industrial refrigeration controls
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Five U.S. agencies warned on Nov. 5 that hackers are targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems worldwide, including controllers used by grocery stores, hospitals, food producers and transport operators. Attackers may exploit unpatched or internet-accessible devices to change temperatures or defrost settings, or prevent operators from seeing temperature readings. Such attacks could spoil stock, compromise storage safety and damage equipment. The warning follows attacks on European supermarkets on Nov. 2 and an incident that altered refrigeration settings at three French blood-service facilities. The U.S. agencies did not say whether refrigeration systems in the United States had been targeted. They urged operators to remove unnecessary internet access, secure remote connections, update firmware, isolate control systems from business networks and set alerts for unsafe temperature changes.

items.title: [proplanta.de] Germany mandates video monitoring at large slaughterhouses handling 90% of animals
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Germany’s parliament approved mandatory video monitoring at large slaughterhouses on Nov. 5, requiring cameras to record the handling and killing of animals at facilities above specified slaughter thresholds. The law covers about 232 of the country’s roughly 4,000 slaughterhouses, which process around 90% of animals slaughtered in Germany. The rules take effect Jan. 1, 2027, and give affected businesses a year to install the equipment. Authorities may also order monitoring at smaller plants when there are specific grounds to suspect animal-welfare violations. Veterinary authorities can access recordings after slaughter, and the footage may be analyzed using artificial intelligence. Parliament also delayed the planned state animal-husbandry label for meat from Jan. 1, 2027, to Oct. 1, 2027, citing the time needed to reform the system.

items.content_html:

Protesters breached the construction site of Microsoft’s planned Amsterdam data center Friday, with around 100 people entering the site. Pure Data Centres is developing the facility, which consists of three towers about 85 meters tall with a capacity of 78 megawatts, for Microsoft as its sole tenant. Dutch police said they detained 150 to 200 people, and one officer was slightly injured. AFP reported that construction stopped for the day. Campaigners say the project’s electricity demand could equal that of Amsterdam’s households, a claim not independently established in the reporting, and argue that the development puts pressure on local power and water supplies. Organizers seek a pause on new large-scale facilities until governments set clearer rules, rather than closure of existing data centers. European Union technology chief Henna Virkkunen has argued that Europe needs data centers to develop its own AI capacity, while saying residents must be protected from higher energy bills, blackouts and environmental damage.

items.title: [bbc.co.uk] Oleshky evacuation moves hundreds out as local ceasefire nears end
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Hundreds of residents left Russian-occupied Oleshky on Friday as Russian and Ukrainian officials completed a joint evacuation and aid operation under a local truce, the first such mission since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion. The ceasefire, brokered with help from U.S. first lady Melania Trump and supported by Pope Leo XIV, allowed food and medical supplies into the frontline town; officials have not confirmed the total number evacuated. People headed for Ukrainian-controlled areas were taken first to Anapa in southern Russia and were then due to fly to Belarus and travel by bus into Ukraine. The circuitous route avoids mined roads along the front line. More than 1,000 residents, many elderly, remained in the town, according to a report from the scene; they received food, medicine, hygiene supplies and fuel. The truce is due to end late Sunday, Nov. 1. The Russian and Ukrainian human rights commissioners have asked Melania Trump to help coordinate recurring relief missions, while peace talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States are expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in early November.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Most U.S. clocks turn back one hour Nov. 1, as new research reviews renew debate over whether year-round standard time or daylight saving time better supports health. A Canadian policy analysis and a review focused on people with mental illness argue that permanent standard time better protects sleep, mood and biological rhythms. A broader review of population studies, however, finds a mix of harms and benefits from seasonal clock changes and summer daylight saving time. Permanent daylight saving time would delay winter sunrise, while permanent standard time would bring earlier summer sunrises and winter sunsets. The U.S. House passed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent in July 2026, but the Senate has not taken it up. The next seasonal clock change is scheduled for March 14, 2027.

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

Its advisory, dated Nov. 5, said financial services and operational technology require particular attention. The team warned that attackers could automate password-based intrusions, disrupt online banking or display false account balances to alarm customers. It urged organizations to monitor unusual login attempts and application programming interface (API) activity, check banking records against customer-facing balances, secure remote access and industrial systems, and review incident-response plans. NCERT cited attacks on European supermarket refrigeration systems as examples of physical and commercial risks to connected systems, but said AI’s involvement in those incidents has not been confirmed.

items.title: [sciencedaily.com] Researchers identify heme in 115-million-year-old Brazilian dinosaur fossil
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

An international research team says it has found mineralized structures resembling red blood cells and heme, a molecule associated with hemoglobin, in a 115-million-year-old Aratasaurus museunacionali fossil from northeastern Brazil. The team describes the findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, as the first chemical confirmation of heme-derived molecules inside structures interpreted as dinosaur blood cells. The team says the structures lay inside the bone’s vascular canals and that the surrounding sediment lacked the same heme signature. It proposes that the mineral hausmannite helped preserve the structures and associated molecules; rapid burial in a low-oxygen setting may also have slowed decay. Paleontologist Mary Schweitzer, who was not involved in the study, disputes whether the evidence definitively identifies heme within the cell-like structures, noting that the chemical analysis covered the whole bone. The researchers say fossilization may have distorted the structures’ shape and that further work is needed to interpret it.
